questions.question: Which black-and-white television sketch has run every New Year's Eve in Germany for decades?
questions.fun_fact: German public broadcaster NDR recorded the English-language sketch in 1963; in Britain itself it is virtually unknown.

questions.question: Where does the German name 'Silvester' for 31 December come from?

answers.text: From a pope who died on that day
From a Latin word for fire

questions.fun_fact: Pope Sylvester I died on 31 December 335, so his feast day landed on the last day of the year.

questions.question: Since when has a lit ball dropped in New York's Times Square at the turn of the year?
questions.fun_fact: Before that the square had fireworks, which the city banned on fire-safety grounds.

questions.question: Which poem is the song 'Auld Lang Syne' based on?
questions.fun_fact: Burns sent the words to a song archive in 1788, saying he had taken them down from an old man.

questions.question: What do Spaniards traditionally eat in the twelve seconds around midnight?
questions.fun_fact: One grape per chime; anyone who chokes or falls behind supposedly forfeits their luck for the year.

questions.question: How did the Spanish twelve-grape custom supposedly start around 1909?

answers.text: Growers in Alicante had a record harvest to sell
A radio station raffled off grapes

questions.fun_fact: The 'uvas de la suerte' began as a marketing idea and became a nationwide habit within a few years.

questions.question: Which clock do people in Madrid gather in front of at the turn of the year?

answers.text: The clock on the Puerta del Sol

questions.fun_fact: The four preliminary chimes before the twelve are part of the ritual; starting early ruins the count.

questions.question: What do many Danes do at the exact moment the year turns?

answers.text: They throw salt over the shoulder

questions.fun_fact: The jump marks the leap into the new year, and broken crockery on your doorstep counts as proof of friendship.

questions.question: What do Japanese households send in their millions at the turn of the year?
questions.fun_fact: 'Nengajo' are collected in advance and delivered by the post office in one batch on New Year's morning.

questions.question: Which dish do many Japanese eat on the evening of 31 December?
questions.fun_fact: 'Toshikoshi soba' break easily between the teeth, which symbolises cutting loose from the old year's troubles.

questions.question: What is the Scottish New Year's Eve festival called?
questions.fun_fact: Because Christmas was long suppressed in Scotland, the big celebration migrated to the turn of the year.

questions.question: What is the Scottish 'first footer' supposed to bring into the house after midnight?
questions.fun_fact: A dark-haired man makes the best first visitor; a fair-haired one used to be read as a warning of trouble.

questions.question: Which pastry belongs to New Year's Eve in the Netherlands?
questions.fun_fact: Legend held that the deep-fried dough balls warded off evil spirits, whose blades slid off the greasy skin.

questions.question: What do tens of thousands of Dutch people do at Scheveningen on 1 January?

answers.text: They plunge into the North Sea

questions.fun_fact: The 'Nieuwjaarsduik' happens in single-digit water temperatures, and pea soup follows by tradition.

questions.question: Which pulse do Italians eat at New Year as a symbol of luck?
questions.fun_fact: Their shape recalls coins, and they are classically served with cotechino or zampone.

questions.question: Which colour is the traditional Italian underwear on New Year's Eve?
questions.fun_fact: It is meant to bring luck and, by tradition, is thrown away on New Year's Day.

questions.question: What is hidden in the Greek 'vasilopita'?
questions.fun_fact: Whoever gets the slice with the coin has luck for the year; the first slice traditionally belongs to the house.

questions.question: Which colour do many Brazilians wear on New Year's Eve?
questions.fun_fact: White stands for peace; on Copacabana many also jump seven waves and throw flowers into the sea.

questions.question: What do many people in Ecuador and Colombia burn at midnight?

answers.text: Home-made effigies representing the old year

questions.fun_fact: The 'años viejos' often wear the faces of politicians or film characters, sometimes with a will in the pocket.

questions.question: Which pattern do many people in the Philippines wear at New Year?
questions.fun_fact: Round shapes stand for coins, which is also why twelve round fruits sit on the table.

questions.question: Which Soviet film traditionally airs in Russia at the turn of the year?
questions.fun_fact: The 1975 comedy has run almost every year for decades and is as much part of the ritual as the sparkling wine.

questions.question: Who traditionally brings the presents at New Year in Russia?

answers.text: Father Frost with his granddaughter Snegurochka

questions.fun_fact: In Soviet times the celebration was deliberately shifted from church Christmas to the turn of the year.

questions.question: Which island state greets the new year among the very first in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Kiribati's Line Islands sit in time zone UTC+14, the earliest that exists.

questions.question: What did Samoa do to its calendar at the end of 2011?
questions.fun_fact: Jumping the date line moved the country closer to Australia and New Zealand, its main trading partners.

questions.question: Which people made the earliest known new-year resolutions about 4,000 years ago?
questions.fun_fact: At the Akitu festival they promised the gods to settle debts and return borrowed tools.

questions.question: Who fixed 1 January as the start of the year in the Roman calendar?
questions.fun_fact: Through the calendar reform of 46 BCE; before that the Roman year began in March.

questions.question: Which pope is today's globally used calendar named after?
questions.fun_fact: The 1582 switch skipped ten days: 4 October was followed immediately by the 15th.

questions.question: When did the official new year begin in England before 1752?
questions.fun_fact: Only the switch to the Gregorian calendar moved the start of the year to 1 January.

questions.question: What is a leap second, usually inserted at the end of the year, for?

answers.text: It keeps atomic time in step with the Earth's rotation

questions.fun_fact: The Earth's rotation is not perfectly steady, and atomic clocks are more precise than the planet they describe.

questions.question: Why do Germans now pour wax rather than lead on New Year's Eve?

answers.text: Because lead-pouring kits were banned in the EU

questions.fun_fact: A limit on lead in consumer products made the classic sets unsellable in 2018.

questions.question: What is a Feuerzangenbowle?

answers.text: A punch with a rum-soaked sugarloaf burning above it
A pastry fried in a pan

questions.fun_fact: The sugarloaf sits in a pair of tongs over the pot and drips caramelised into the wine.

questions.question: Which New Year's Eve prank involving doughnuts is common in Germany?

answers.text: One is filled with mustard instead of jam

questions.fun_fact: Tradition says whoever gets the mustard doughnut still has luck in the coming year.

questions.question: Which piece traditionally closes the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert?
questions.fun_fact: The audience claps along, and the conductor spends the piece conducting the hall rather than the orchestra.

questions.question: Which waltz opens the encores at the Vienna New Year's Concert?
questions.fun_fact: The orchestra is interrupted after the opening bars so the players can wish the audience a good year.

questions.question: Roughly what pressure sits inside a sealed champagne bottle?
questions.fun_fact: That is roughly three times a car tyre, which is why the glass is thick and the cork is wired down.

questions.question: When may a sparkling wine be called champagne?

answers.text: Only if it comes from the Champagne region
Only if it ages at least ten years
Only if it is made from a single grape variety

questions.fun_fact: France defends the protected designation of origin in courts around the world.

questions.question: What is 'sabrage' with a bottle of sparkling wine?

answers.text: Striking the neck off with a sabre

questions.fun_fact: The blow lands on the seam of the bottle, and the internal pressure blows off the glass ring with the cork.

questions.question: In which country were fireworks invented?
questions.fun_fact: Black powder was first used to scare off evil spirits with noise; the colours came centuries later.

questions.question: What produces the colour red in a firework?
questions.fun_fact: Copper burns blue, barium green and sodium yellow: fireworks are applied flame chemistry.

questions.question: On how many days a year may New Year fireworks normally be sold in Germany?
questions.fun_fact: Sales are limited to 29–31 December, and the start shifts if one of those days falls on a Sunday.

questions.question: Which readings spike in European cities during the New Year's Eve night?
questions.fun_fact: In the first hour of the year they often sit at a multiple of the daily limit.

questions.question: Between which dates can Chinese New Year fall?
questions.fun_fact: The Chinese calendar is lunisolar, and the festival falls on the second new moon after the winter solstice.

questions.question: When does the Persian new year festival Nowruz begin?

answers.text: At the first full moon in February

questions.fun_fact: Nowruz is celebrated from Iran to Central Asia and is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.

questions.question: In which month does Ethiopia celebrate its new year, 'Enkutatash'?
questions.fun_fact: The Ethiopian calendar has thirteen months: twelve of 30 days and one short remainder month.

questions.question: How does Thailand mark its new year at 'Songkran'?
questions.fun_fact: The originally ritual pouring of water for purification is now a three-day April water festival.

questions.question: Which problem preoccupied the IT world at the turn of 1999 to 2000?
questions.fun_fact: Because '00' could read as 1900, billions went into fixing it worldwide — and very little happened.

questions.question: Which poem is read out at Skansen in Sweden at the turn of the year?
questions.fun_fact: The tradition dates from 1895 and the recitation is broadcast nationwide on television.

questions.question: Which meat do Hungarians avoid on New Year's Day?
questions.fun_fact: Superstition says the luck would fly away; pork, by contrast, roots forwards and brings progress.

questions.question: What are Irish households said to do with a loaf of bread at New Year?

answers.text: Bang it against walls and doors

questions.fun_fact: The noise is meant to drive misfortune out of the house and good bread into the coming year.

questions.question: What is smashed on the doorstep at New Year in Turkey and Greece?
questions.fun_fact: The further the seeds scatter, the greater the blessing on the house is supposed to be.

questions.question: Which colour is the lucky New Year underwear in Peru and parts of Latin America?
questions.fun_fact: Yellow stands for prosperity; those hoping for love choose red instead.

questions.question: What do Mexicans do with an empty suitcase at New Year?

answers.text: Walk around the block with it

questions.fun_fact: The walk is meant to secure travel in the coming year; some go only to the corner and back.

questions.question: Which salad is a fixture on the Russian New Year's Eve table?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after a chef who invented it in 19th-century Moscow, and the original recipe is considered lost.

questions.question: Which television programme do nearly all Icelanders watch on New Year's Eve?

answers.text: A concert from the Harpa hall
A live feed from the geysers

questions.fun_fact: The streets empty for half an hour, and only afterwards do the fireworks and bonfires start.

questions.question: What takes place in Madrid on the afternoon of 31 December?
questions.fun_fact: The 'San Silvestre Vallecana' draws tens of thousands, and many run in costume.

questions.question: Which band released the song 'Happy New Year' in 1980?
questions.fun_fact: The lyric is far more melancholy than the title suggests, and in several countries it only charted years later.

questions.question: Where does the month name January come from?

answers.text: From the Latin word for ice

questions.fun_fact: Janus has two faces and looks backwards and forwards at once, which is hard to improve on for a year's start.

questions.question: What does the German toast 'Prosit Neujahr' literally mean?
questions.fun_fact: 'Prosit' is Latin and entered German through 18th-century student slang.

questions.question: Which sporting event traditionally takes place in Germany on 1 January?

answers.text: The New Year ski jumping in Garmisch-Partenkirchen

questions.fun_fact: It is the second stop of the Four Hills Tournament and starts with qualifying in the morning.

questions.question: Which flower parade takes place in California on New Year's Day?

answers.text: The Poppy Parade in San Diego

questions.fun_fact: Every float must be covered entirely in plant material, down to the last leaf.

questions.question: Who made 'Auld Lang Syne' a fixture of the North American New Year?
questions.fun_fact: His orchestra played it live at midnight every year from 1929, first on radio and later on television.

questions.question: What is the Welsh 'Mari Lwyd' that travels door to door around New Year?

answers.text: A decorated horse skull on a pole
A straw doll in a boat

questions.fun_fact: The party demands entry in rhyming verse, and the household has to answer in rhyme.

questions.question: Which country greets the new year among the last in the world?

answers.text: The United States, with Baker and Howland Islands

questions.fun_fact: The uninhabited islands sit in time zone UTC−12, a full 26 hours behind Kiribati.

questions.question: What is thrown out of the window at midnight in parts of Cuba and Puerto Rico?
questions.fun_fact: The water is meant to wash the old year's bad luck out of the house.

questions.question: What do the men in Stonehaven, Scotland, swing through the streets at New Year?

answers.text: Burning wire cages on long chains

questions.fun_fact: The fireballs end up in the harbour, and the custom is meant to drive off evil spirits.

questions.question: What is the Scottish New Year dip into the freezing Firth of Forth called?
questions.fun_fact: Many take the plunge in costume, and the event raises money for charity.

questions.question: Which structure marks the turn of the year in Sydney with one of the world's first big firework displays?
questions.fun_fact: Because of the time zone, pictures from Sydney often reach Europe on the afternoon of 31 December.

questions.question: At which landmark does Berlin traditionally hold its biggest New Year's Eve party?
questions.fun_fact: The stage show on the 'party mile' is broadcast live on television.

questions.question: Which building is at the centre of Dubai's New Year's Eve fireworks?
questions.fun_fact: The facade of the world's tallest building doubles as a projection screen.

questions.question: On which beach does one of the world's biggest New Year's Eve parties take place?
questions.fun_fact: Millions arrive dressed in white, and after the fireworks flowers go into the water for the sea goddess Iemanjá.

questions.question: What happens to the slips of paper visitors write their wishes on at Times Square?

answers.text: They are dropped as confetti at midnight
They are archived at city hall

questions.fun_fact: The wishes are collected beforehand and tipped off the rooftops with the rest of the confetti.

questions.question: How long does the Times Square ball take to complete its descent?
questions.fun_fact: It reaches the bottom precisely at midnight, and the numerals of the new year light up only afterwards.

questions.question: Where does the German greeting 'Guten Rutsch' probably come from?

answers.text: From an old word for a good journey

questions.fun_fact: The popular derivation from Yiddish is regarded by linguists as doubtful.

questions.question: Which figure symbolises the new year in many countries?

answers.text: A baby wearing a sash with the year on it

questions.fun_fact: The motif is centuries old and was popularised by magazine covers from the 19th century onwards.

questions.question: What is a Scandinavian 'kransekake'?
questions.fun_fact: The rings shrink from bottom to top, and at New Year a small flag often sits on the summit.

questions.question: How many meals does Estonian tradition prescribe on New Year's Eve?
questions.fun_fact: Those are the lucky numbers, and the eater is said to gain the strength of that many men.

questions.question: What do many Japanese do in the first days of the year at 'hatsumode'?

answers.text: They make the year's first visit to a shrine or temple
They cast a poem into the sea

questions.fun_fact: Old lucky charms are handed back on the same visit and new ones bought.

questions.question: What are Japanese 'otoshidama'?

answers.text: Money gifts for children in small envelopes
New Year poems on rice paper

questions.fun_fact: The amount depends on age, with older children receiving more.

questions.question: Which soup do Koreans eat on New Year's Day?

answers.text: A soup with sliced rice cakes
A soup with seaweed and clams

questions.fun_fact: Tradition says you only turn a year older once you have eaten 'tteokguk'.

questions.question: What is the Vietnamese new year festival called?
questions.fun_fact: It follows the lunar calendar and usually coincides with Chinese New Year; kumquat trees belong in every home.

questions.question: What is blown to mark the Jewish new year, Rosh Hashanah?
questions.fun_fact: The shofar is sounded in a fixed sequence of calls, and the festival falls in autumn.

questions.question: Why does the Islamic new year drift through the seasons?

answers.text: Because the Islamic calendar is purely lunar
Because it is tied to Easter
Because it is shifted every four years

questions.fun_fact: The lunar year is about eleven days shorter than the solar one, so 1 Muharram moves forward each year.

questions.question: Until when was Christmas Day not a general public holiday in Scotland?
questions.fun_fact: That is why Hogmanay was for centuries the real winter celebration there.

questions.question: What classically appears on the table for the French 'Réveillon de la Saint-Sylvestre'?
questions.fun_fact: Foie gras and champagne usually join them, and the meal starts late and runs long.

questions.question: What is a Belgian New Year custom for children?

answers.text: They read a letter they wrote to their godparents
They ring cowbells in the fields
They hide coins in the snow

questions.fun_fact: The letter is written on decorated paper and read out ceremonially on New Year's Day.

questions.question: What happens at the Appenzell 'Silvesterchlausen' in Switzerland?

answers.text: Groups in elaborate costumes go farm to farm and yodel
A burning wheel is rolled down the mountain

questions.fun_fact: It happens twice: on 31 December and again on 13 January, following the old calendar.

questions.question: What is a 'cotillón' at a Spanish or Latin American New Year's party?

answers.text: A bag of hats, horns and streamers

questions.fun_fact: After the twelve grapes the bag is opened and the noise starts.

questions.question: What is thrown out of office windows in Argentina on the last working day of the year?
questions.fun_fact: The paper storm in the financial district of Buenos Aires makes the news every year.

questions.question: Where does the word 'confetti' come from?

answers.text: From a Latin word for wind

questions.fun_fact: Milanese carnival crowds once threw sweets; when that got too expensive, coloured paper took their place.

questions.question: Why was 1900 not a leap year?

answers.text: Full centuries are leap years only when divisible by 400
Because the calendar was reformed that year

questions.fun_fact: The same rule drops 2100, while 2000 did qualify.

questions.question: What is sung in the Vatican on the evening of 31 December?

answers.text: The Te Deum, as a service of thanksgiving

questions.fun_fact: The pope gives thanks for the closing year; 1 January is then the World Day of Peace.

questions.question: When does the Danish head of state give the new year address?
questions.fun_fact: The 6 p.m. speech structures the evening: dinner before, celebration after.

questions.question: What is the Dutch 'oudejaarsconference'?

answers.text: A comedian's satirical review of the year

questions.fun_fact: The show often runs beyond two hours and airs live on the evening of 31 December.

questions.question: Which ball season traditionally opens in Vienna around the turn of the year?
questions.fun_fact: The Imperial Ball at the Hofburg takes place on New Year's Eve; the Opera Ball follows only in February.

questions.question: How many animal signs does the Chinese zodiac, which gives each year a sign, contain?
questions.fun_fact: The rat comes first; legend says the cat arrived too late for the race and is missing as a result.

questions.question: How many grapes do people in Spain eat to the chimes on New Year's Eve?
questions.fun_fact: Twelve, one per chime — which is why shops sell them peeled and de-seeded in tins.

questions.question: How many times do Japanese temple bells ring on the night before New Year's Day?
questions.fun_fact: The 108 strikes stand for the worldly desires left behind with the old year.

questions.question: How many hours pass between the first and the last turn of the year on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: 26 hours — from UTC+14 in Kiribati's Line Islands to UTC−12 at Baker and Howland Islands.

questions.question: In which year did Pope Gregory XIII introduce the calendar used worldwide today?
questions.fun_fact: 1582 — in the changeover, 4 October was followed directly by 15 October.

questions.question: In which year did German broadcaster NDR record the sketch 'Dinner for One' that has run at New Year ever since?
questions.fun_fact: 1963 — taped before a live audience in Hamburg, in English and without subtitles.
